name: Jude
author: The writer calls himself Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, usually taken to be the James who led the church in Jerusalem and was himself a brother of Jesus. Traditionally Jude is identified as one of the brothers of Jesus named in the Gospels. Jesus' brothers did not believe in him during his ministry, but they are found among the believers after the resurrection, and Paul mentions the Lord's brothers travelling as missionaries. Beyond this, little is known about Jude himself. Many scholars accept the traditional view, while others think a later follower wrote in Jude's name to carry his authority.
audience: The letter does not name its readers. They were probably believers steeped in Jewish Scripture and tradition, perhaps in Palestine or nearby, meeting in small house churches. Certain people had slipped into their gatherings, sharing their meals while living immorally and treating God's grace as a licence for it, and Jude writes urgently to warn the believers about them.
era: Scholars date Jude anywhere from around AD 50–70, if Jude himself wrote it, to around AD 90 or a little later, if it was written in his name. The young church was spreading across the Roman Empire through small household congregations, often visited by travelling teachers whose claims were hard to check. Letters like this one were carried by messengers and read aloud when believers gathered.

notes.1:5: In this passage Jude reminds his readers of stories they already knew. Some come from the Old Testament, such as Israel's escape from Egypt. Others come from popular Jewish writings outside the Old Testament: later in the passage he mentions a tradition about the archangel Michael disputing over the body of Moses, and words from 1 Enoch, an ancient Jewish book written in the name of Enoch, the early ancestor listed in Genesis.
